Title: Voluntary Free Speech: Ensuring a Sustainable Digital Ecosystem

Introduction

An ever-evolving digital landscape has redefined virtually every aspect of human life, and with that paradigm shift comes the pressing need to revisit and reassess fundamental rights, values and liberties. Of these, none is more important than the freedom of expression, long enshrined as a cornerstone of democratic societies and protected by constitutions, laws, and international legal norms. In recent years, however, the reliance of the modern world on social media and tech platforms has led to growing concerns about content moderation, censorship, and selective enforcement. The argument that follows seeks to make an impassioned case for abolishing all content moderation by social media and tech platforms, advocating instead for a legally binding requirement that they host all lawful speech without exception. Only such a standard will guarantee the continued sanctity of free expression in the age of information and communication technologies.

The Case Against Content Moderation

Content moderation, as currently practiced by social media and tech platforms, is a fundamentally flawed and inherently subjective mechanism for regulating online communication. Vague and inadequately defined community standards and content policies give these private entities free rein to selectively suppress, demonetize, and delete voices with little or no oversight, transparency, or accountability. Furthermore, these entities may also silence unpopular opinions and favor the proliferation of certain ideologies, to the detriment of pluralism and democratic discourse.

Importantly, content moderation is rife with inconsistencies as moderators struggle to apply complex policies and guidelines, grappling with various languages, cultural contexts, and political sensitivities. This can lead to inadvertent violations of user rights, while simultaneously failing to address legitimate concerns like hate speech, harassment, and incitement to violence. It is high time these platforms relinquished authority over user content and embraced an absolutist approach to free expression, in which lawful speech is permitted without exception.

Protecting Minority Voices and Fostering Digital Democracy

Current content moderation practices disempower minority voices and hinder the development of a healthy online public square. The fear of arbitrary censorship often leads to self-censorship, preventing marginalized individuals and groups from using digital platforms to share their experiences, advocate for their rights, and engage in public debate.

Abolishing content moderation and mandating that all lawful speech be hosted would help rectify these systemic biases, encouraging the fruitful exchange of ideas, knowledge, and perspectives that lie at the heart of democratic societies. By leveling the playing field, users from diverse backgrounds will be empowered to participate, to express themselves freely, and to engage in civic discourse.

Promoting Innovation and Competition

Free expression is foundational for fostering innovation and competition in the digital realm. Content moderation practices have been criticized for creating an imbalanced market in which a handful of tech giants wield enormous power over information flows. Requiring platforms to host all lawful speech would disrupt this oligopoly and stimulate greater innovation and competition in the tech industry. This would pave the way for new, more ethical, and democratic platforms to emerge that champion user empowerment, privacy, and freedom.

Tackling Lawful but Unwanted Speech: A Shared Responsibility

Abolishing content moderation does not imply a laissez-faire approach to regulating online spaces. Lawful speech that is deemed harmful, offensive, or unwanted must be addressed through collective responsibility - a shared effort by governments, civil society, and individual users – placing emphasis on education, digital literacy, and resilience.

Harnessing empowering tools such as user-controlled content filters, preferences, and customizable algorithms, users will be entrusted with the autonomy to decide what content they want to be exposed to or shielded from, without being manipulated or dictated by unaccountable tech platforms.

Conclusion

In summary, the call to abolish content moderation by social media and tech platforms is a plea for upholding and safeguarding absolute free expression online. By legally requiring these platforms to host all lawful speech, the digital space will become innovative, equitable, and more democratic. Acknowledging and embracing the communal nature of the internet and its influential role in our lives, the responsibility for maintaining a healthy online environment shifts from opaque tech giants to a more distributed and collaborative network, invigorating and sustaining the freedom of expression that is prerequisite to an open and pluriform society.

  2. Preventing bias and discrimination: A lack of content moderation would mean that social media platforms cannot exercise any form of discrimination or bias when it comes to the content they host.   6. Protecting minority voices: Content moderation can sometimes lead to the silencing of minority voices or marginalized groups, whose perspectives may be deemed controversial or unpalatable by the platform. Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for enacting laws that prohibit social media platforms from engaging in any form of content moderation, thereby mandating they host all legal content and act as neutral common carriers upholding absolute freedom of speech.
Model Response:

Overview

A number of legislators, advocacy groups, and commentators argue that social‑media companies should be treated as “neutral common carriers” that are prohibited from exercising any form of editorial judgment over user‑generated content. In this view, platforms would be required to host every piece of speech that is legal under existing law and would be barred from removing, demoting, or otherwise moderating that content. Below is a summary of the main reasons and benefits that proponents cite for such a regulatory approach, followed by a brief note on the broader policy debate.

1. Protection of Free Speech

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Absolute freedom of expression By removing the ability of private platforms to edit or delete lawful speech, individuals are guaranteed an unrestricted outlet for their ideas, opinions, and information.
Prevention of “private censorship” Proponents argue that platforms, as private companies, currently act as gatekeepers and can suppress views they find disagreeable, thereby undermining the First Amendment principle that government (not private actors) should not limit speech.
Marketplace of ideas An unrestricted flow of all legal content is believed to allow the best ideas to rise to the top through genuine public debate rather than through algorithmic or editorial choices made by a corporate entity.

2. Limiting Corporate Power and Bias

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Checks on corporate discretion Without a legal right to moderate, companies cannot unilaterally shape public discourse, which some see as an overreach of private power.
Neutrality across political viewpoints A common‑carrier model is presented as a way to guarantee that no political ideology receives preferential treatment, reducing accusations of partisan bias.
Transparency and predictability Users would know that any legal content they post will remain accessible, creating a more predictable environment for speech and for businesses that rely on platform distribution.

3. Legal Consistency and Clarity

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Uniform standard (legal vs. illegal) The rule would reduce ambiguity: platforms would only need to remove content that is illegal (e.g., child sexual abuse material, threats of violence); everything else would stay.
Alignment with existing common‑carrier regime Proponents point to precedents in telecommunications (e.g., the Communications Act’s “common carrier” definition) as a model for treating internet services similarly, arguing that this provides a clear statutory framework.
Reduced litigation over moderation decisions If platforms are barred from moderating, they would face fewer lawsuits alleging wrongful removal or suppression of speech.

4. Encouraging Innovation and Competition

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Level playing field All platforms would operate under the same non‑moderation rule, preventing any single company from gaining a competitive edge through aggressive content curation.
User‑driven curation Without platform‑controlled moderation, users could develop third‑party tools (browser extensions, community filters) to tailor their own experiences, spurring a market for “personalized moderation” services.
Lower barriers for new entrants Smaller or niche platforms might find it easier to launch if they are not required to build large, costly moderation teams; they would simply inherit the legal‑only‑removal requirement.

5. International and Human‑Rights Signaling

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Alignment with global free‑speech norms Advocates claim that a non‑moderating regime mirrors the strongest interpretations of free‑speech protections found in liberal democracies and international human‑rights instruments.
Countering “information control” by authoritarian states By insisting that U.S. platforms cannot filter lawful content, proponents argue the United States would set a global example against state‑backed internet censorship.

6. Reducing “Shadow Bans” and Algorithmic Opacity

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Eliminates hidden down‑ranking Critics of current moderation say platforms quietly demote certain posts or accounts (“shadow bans”) without notice. A no‑moderation rule would make any reduction in reach transparent (i.e., any reduction would have to be due to technical issues, not editorial decisions).
Simplifies platform accountability If platforms cannot modify distribution, audits of their systems become simpler because the only actions they can take are removal of illegal content—an activity that is already subject to legal reporting requirements.

7. Ethical and Philosophical Arguments

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Moral principle of non‑interference Some ethicists argue that the state should not compel private entities to act as moral arbiters; letting speech flow unimpeded respects individual autonomy.
Avoiding “digital paternalism” The idea is that users are capable of deciding for themselves what to read or ignore, and the platform should not act as a paternalistic guardian deciding what is “good” or “bad” for the public.

8. Potential Economic Advantages

Reason How It Is Cast as a Benefit
Reduced operational costs for moderation Large moderation staffs, AI‑based content‑filtering systems, and legal review processes are expensive. Removing the requirement could lower operating expenditures and, in theory, translate into lower service fees or higher profits.
Higher ad revenues from larger audiences With no content removal, the user base could be larger and more engaged, potentially increasing advertising impressions and overall revenue.

Brief Note on the Broader Debate

While the points above capture the reasons and benefits that supporters of a “no‑moderation” law typically advance, the policy conversation also includes substantial counter‑arguments (e.g., concerns about hate speech, disinformation, harassment, platform liability, and public safety). In many jurisdictions, lawmakers and courts balance the desire for robust free speech with the need to protect individuals and societies from illegal or harmful content. Whether a common‑carrier approach that eliminates all moderation is feasible or desirable remains a contested political question, and many proposals include nuanced exemptions (e.g., for illegal content, child exploitation material, or threats of imminent violence) to address those concerns.

Takeaway: Proponents of prohibiting content moderation view such laws as a way to ensure absolute legal speech, curb corporate editorial power, provide legal clarity, foster competition, protect against censorship, and uphold a principled commitment to free expression. Whether those anticipated benefits materialize, and at what social cost, is the central point of ongoing public and legislative debate.

Absolute Free Expression Online: A Case for Abolishing Content Moderation

In today’s digital age, the internet has become the modern public square—a space where ideas, opinions, and debates should flow freely without undue interference. Yet, in many corners of this virtual realm, private social media and tech platforms have taken upon themselves the role of gatekeepers, enforcing rules and policies that often lead to selective censorship. To safeguard the fundamental right to free expression, it is imperative that we abolish all forms of content moderation by these platforms and establish legal mandates requiring them to host all lawful speech without bias or arbitrary enforcement.

The Perils of Private Censorship

Social media companies, while private entities, wield enormous influence over public discourse. Their content moderation policies are frequently opaque, inconsistent, and driven by corporate interests or political pressures rather than objective legal standards. This unchecked power results in several critical issues:

  • Arbitrary Enforcement: Moderation decisions are often made behind closed doors, leaving users confused about why certain posts are removed or shadow-banned while others remain. This lack of transparency undermines trust and stifles open dialogue.
  • Selective Censorship: When platforms decide what content is acceptable, they inherently prioritize certain viewpoints over others. This selective enforcement creates an uneven playing field, where dissenting or unpopular opinions are disproportionately suppressed.
  • Chilling Effect on Debate: The fear of being censored can deter individuals from expressing controversial or innovative ideas. In an era where robust debate is essential for progress, this chilling effect hampers the free exchange of ideas and limits societal growth.

Upholding the Principle of Free Speech

The cornerstone of any democratic society is the unassailable right to free expression. By legally requiring tech platforms to host all lawful speech, we reinforce this principle in a manner that is both clear and robust:

  • Protection of Minority Voices: Absolute free expression ensures that even the most controversial or minority viewpoints have a chance to be heard. When platforms are not allowed to arbitrarily filter content, all voices—regardless of their popularity—can contribute to the national conversation.
  • Accountability and Transparency: A legal framework that mandates the hosting of all lawful speech would compel companies to operate with greater transparency. Clear guidelines and judicial oversight would replace capricious decisions, ensuring that the public can hold platforms accountable for any misuse of power.
  • Empowerment of the Public: When individuals know that their lawful speech will not be subject to unwarranted censorship, they are more likely to participate actively in public discourse. This empowerment is essential for a vibrant democracy where ideas are contested and refined through open debate.

Addressing Concerns Without Compromising Free Expression

Critics of abolishing content moderation may argue that some level of moderation is necessary to prevent hate speech, misinformation, and harassment. However, these concerns can—and should—be addressed through well-defined legal frameworks rather than through the discretionary practices of private companies:

  • Legal Boundaries over Private Judgment: Existing laws already prohibit speech that incites violence or constitutes hate speech. Rather than relying on the subjective decisions of tech companies, these issues can be managed through transparent legal processes that respect due process and evidence-based adjudication.
  • Narrowing the Scope of Enforcement: A legal mandate to host all lawful speech would only permit intervention when content clearly violates established laws. This distinction preserves the right to free expression while still protecting the public from genuinely harmful content.
  • Judicial Oversight and Remedies: By placing the responsibility for regulating speech in the hands of the legal system, rather than private entities, we ensure that any restrictions are subject to rigorous judicial review. This accountability is crucial in maintaining a balance between safety and freedom.

The Road to an Open Digital Public Square

The digital public square should be a realm where ideas are contested on their merit rather than filtered through the lens of corporate policy. Abolishing content moderation on social media and tech platforms would:

  • Eradicate Unfair Bias: Eliminating arbitrary moderation would remove the undue influence of corporate interests on public discourse, thereby ensuring that the marketplace of ideas remains truly competitive and diverse.
  • Encourage Innovation and Debate: Without the fear of being censored, innovators, activists, and citizens alike would feel empowered to share unconventional or challenging perspectives. This environment is essential for the progress of knowledge and the evolution of societal norms.
  • Restore Trust in Digital Platforms: Transparency in how content is handled is key to rebuilding public trust. A legal framework that guarantees the hosting of all lawful speech would not only protect free expression but also foster a more accountable and fair digital ecosystem.

Conclusion

Absolute free expression online is not merely an ideal; it is a fundamental right that underpins the health and vitality of any modern democracy. The practice of content moderation by private social media and tech platforms has proven to be a double-edged sword—while it may aim to curb harmful content, it also risks stifling legitimate discourse and perpetuating bias. To protect every lawful voice and ensure that ideas can flourish without undue interference, it is essential to abolish all forms of content moderation and legally require these platforms to host all lawful speech.

By shifting the responsibility of regulating speech to transparent, accountable legal institutions, we can create an online environment where free expression is truly absolute. In doing so, we uphold the democratic principles that have long been the foundation of an open society and empower every individual to participate fully in the digital public square.

When discussing the idea of enacting laws that prohibit social media platforms from engaging in any form of content moderation—thus requiring them to host all legal content and operate as neutral common carriers—several supposed benefits and reasons are often cited by proponents. Here’s an overview of these arguments:

1. Protection of Free Speech

  • Unrestricted Expression: Advocates argue that such laws would guarantee that all legal expressions are available without interference. The idea is that if platforms are forced to host all legal content, users won’t be subject to arbitrary removals that can stifle free expression.
  • Reducing Private Censorship: By limiting the power of private companies to decide which content is allowed, these laws are seen as a way to protect individuals from biased or politically motivated censorship enforced by platforms that have significant control over public discourse.

2. Ensuring Equality and Fairness

  • Neutral Platforms: Mandating neutrality is intended to ensure that all viewpoints, regardless of their popularity or political alignment, have an equal opportunity to be heard. This can be seen as a way to democratize the public sphere.
  • Leveling the Playing Field: Proponents claim that such rules would reduce the concentration of power held by a few large platforms, potentially fostering a more competitive and diverse ecosystem of online communication.

3. Transparency and Consistency

  • Clear Legal Standards: A law that prohibits content moderation (except for content that is illegal) may be seen as establishing a clear, uniform standard of what is allowed. This could lead to greater transparency in how platforms operate.
  • Reducing Arbitrary Decisions: By limiting the discretion available to platforms, supporters argue that it would minimize subjective judgments and the potential for inconsistent application of rules across different communities and topics.

4. Protection of Minority and Dissenting Voices

  • Preventing Silencing: Critics of current moderation practices often argue that dominant platforms may inadvertently (or deliberately) suppress minority or dissenting opinions. A legal requirement to host all legal content could protect these voices from being marginalized.
  • Avoiding the Chilling Effect: When users fear that their content might be removed without clear reason, they may self-censor. Eliminating moderation (beyond what is legally required) could reduce this chilling effect and encourage more open discourse.

5. Accountability and Legal Consistency

  • Uniform Enforcement: Enacting such laws could create a more consistent legal framework for online speech, reducing the variability that can arise when different platforms set their own policies.
  • Clarifying Legal Boundaries: By clearly defining what constitutes legal content, the law could help clarify boundaries for both users and platforms, potentially reducing legal ambiguity and disputes.

Additional Considerations:

While these arguments highlight the potential benefits of a law mandating absolute neutrality for social media platforms, it is important to note the following challenges and controversies:

  • Risk of Harmful Content: Absolute freedom of speech might also lead to the proliferation of hate speech, misinformation, and extremist content. Moderation, even when imperfect, is often seen as necessary to prevent harm.
  • Balancing Free Speech and Safety: Many experts argue that a balance must be struck between protecting free expression and ensuring community safety. Unrestricted hosting of all legal content could complicate efforts to protect vulnerable groups and maintain public order.
  • Practical Implementation: Defining "legal content" clearly and managing the vast volume of online material presents significant regulatory and technical challenges. Determining what should remain on the platform without moderation could be complex and contentious.
  • Unintended Consequences: There is concern that forcing neutrality might lead to platforms becoming conduits for harmful content, which could have broader societal impacts. Critics suggest that some level of moderation is necessary to maintain a safe online environment.

Absolute Free Expression: The Case for Abolishing Content Moderation

Introduction

In the digital age, social media and tech platforms have become the primary avenues for public discourse, news dissemination, and social interaction. However, these platforms have increasingly taken on the role of arbiters of speech, deciding what can and cannot be said online. This essay argues for the abolition of all content moderation by social media and tech platforms, and the legal requirement for them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement. Such a move would guarantee absolute free expression online, fostering a more open, diverse, and democratically vibrant digital ecosystem.

The Fundamental Importance of Free Speech

Free speech is a cornerstone of democratic societies. It allows for the open exchange of ideas, fosters innovation, and ensures that diverse viewpoints are heard. In a world where online platforms have become the modern public square, ensuring that all lawful speech is protected is crucial. By abolishing content moderation, we can safeguard the fundamental right to free expression, allowing individuals to engage in discourse without fear of censorship.

The Dangers of Content Moderation

Content moderation, as currently practiced by social media and tech platforms, is fraught with issues. One of the primary concerns is the lack of transparency and consistency in enforcement. Platforms often rely on complex algorithms and human moderators to remove content, leading to inconsistent application of rules. This opacity can breed mistrust and suspicion, as users are often left in the dark about why their content was removed or their accounts suspended.

Moreover, moderation policies are susceptible to political and ideological biases. Tech companies can easily fall into the trap of enforcing rules that align with their own corporate values or that satisfy political pressures rather than basing decisions on objective criteria. This results in the suppression of unpopular but lawful views, effectively creating echo chambers where only certain perspectives are allowed.

Legal Accountability and Liability Protection

One argument against abolishing content moderation is that platforms would be legally liable for hosting illegal content. However, existing legal frameworks like Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act in the United States provide platforms with immunity from liability for user-generated content. By keeping such protections in place while requiring platforms to host all lawful speech, we can balance the need for free expression with the legal responsibilities of platforms.

Platforms should be held accountable for illegal content, such as incitement to violence, child exploitation, and other unlawful activities. However, this accountability should not extend to lawful but controversial speech. By maintaining the distinction between illegal and merely controversial content, we can protect free expression while ensuring platforms remain safe spaces for legal content.

Encouraging Market Solutions and User Empowerment

Abolishing content moderation would also encourage the development of market-driven solutions for fostering constructive online discourse. Users could choose platforms based on their moderation policies, fostering a more diverse ecosystem where different platforms cater to different audiences. This would create a competitive landscape where platforms succeed or fail based on their ability to provide a user experience that aligns with the values and preferences of their users.

Furthermore, empowering users with tools to filter and curate their own content feeds could be a viable alternative to centralized moderation. Users could block content they find objectionable or follow communities that align with their interests, creating a personalized experience that respects their autonomy and preferences.

Conclusion

The abolition of content moderation and the legal requirement for social media and tech platforms to host all lawful speech without censorship is essential for preserving absolute free expression online. By eliminating the subjectivity and inconsistency inherent in current moderation practices, we can create a more transparent, diverse, and inclusive digital environment. This move would reinforce the fundamental rights enshrined in democratic societies, ensuring that the digital public square remains a bastion of open discourse and innovation.

The Digital Public Square Belongs to the People: The Case for Ending Platform Censorship

Introduction

For most of human history, the freedom to speak was constrained by kings, churches, and states. The great achievement of liberal democracy was wresting control of expression away from centralized authorities and vesting it in the people themselves. Yet in the twenty-first century, a new class of gatekeepers has quietly assumed powers of censorship that no government in a free society could constitutionally exercise. A handful of private corporations—accountable to no electorate, governed by no constitution, and operating behind opaque algorithms and shifting "community standards"—now decide what billions of human beings may say, see, and share. This arrangement is incompatible with a free society. The solution is clear: content moderation by social media and technology platforms should be abolished, and these platforms should be legally required to carry all lawful speech, neutrally and without selective enforcement. Anything less leaves the most important communications infrastructure in history under the arbitrary control of a tiny corporate oligarchy.

The Internet Is the Public Square—and It Must Be Treated Like One

The Supreme Court recognized in Packingham v. North Carolina (2017) that social media platforms constitute "the modern public square"—the principal place where citizens debate politics, petition officials, organize movements, seek employment, and participate in civic life. When the town square was a physical plaza, no private party could banish a citizen from public discourse entirely. Today, exclusion from major platforms amounts to functional exile from public life. A person deplatformed by two or three companies loses access to the dominant channels of political speech, commerce, and community.

When private entities control infrastructure essential to public life, the law has never treated them as ordinary businesses free to discriminate at will. Telephone companies cannot disconnect customers for expressing unpopular views. The postal service cannot refuse to deliver controversial newsletters. Railroads, electric utilities, and internet service providers operate under common carrier obligations precisely because their gatekeeping power over essential services is too dangerous to leave unconstrained. Social media platforms—which enjoy network effects so powerful that meaningful competition is nearly impossible—are the common carriers of speech in the digital age. They should bear the same obligation of neutral carriage that we have long imposed on every other communications utility.

Concentrated Private Censorship Is More Dangerous Than Government Censorship

Defenders of moderation often respond that the First Amendment restrains only governments, not companies. This is legally true and morally beside the point. The purpose of free speech protections is to prevent any concentrated power from controlling public discourse. When two or three corporations control the channels through which the overwhelming majority of political communication flows, the formal identity of the censor matters far less than the fact of censorship.

Indeed, private censorship is in some respects worse than state censorship. Government restrictions on speech must survive judicial scrutiny, public debate, and democratic accountability. Platform censorship occurs in secret, by algorithm, without due process, without appeal to any neutral arbiter, and without any obligation to explain itself. A citizen silenced by the state can sue; a citizen silenced by a platform receives a form email—or nothing at all.

Worse still, private moderation has become a laundering mechanism for government censorship. Litigation and journalism in recent years have revealed extensive "jawboning"—officials pressuring platforms to suppress disfavored speech and speakers, achieving through informal coercion what the Constitution forbids them to do directly. Abolishing discretionary moderation closes this back door. If platforms must carry all lawful speech, governments lose the ability to censor by proxy.

Moderation at Scale Is Inevitably Arbitrary, Biased, and Wrong

Even granting platforms the best intentions, content moderation at the scale of billions of posts per day cannot be done fairly. It is performed by overworked contractors and error-prone algorithms applying vague rules to content stripped of context. The results are predictable: satire flagged as hate speech, war-crimes documentation deleted as violent content, medical discussions removed as misinformation, and activists silenced for quoting the very abuse they oppose.

And the record shows that moderators' confident judgments about truth have repeatedly been wrong. The hypothesis that COVID-19 emerged from a laboratory was banned as misinformation—until it became a mainstream position taken seriously by federal agencies. A major newspaper's accurate reporting was throttled and blocked weeks before a presidential election—a decision platform executives later admitted was a mistake. Claims labeled false have become accepted; claims labeled true have collapsed. Each episode teaches the same lesson: no institution possesses the epistemic authority to adjudicate truth for an entire society, and the attempt to do so corrupts the process of inquiry by which truth is actually discovered.

Selective enforcement compounds the injury. Identical conduct is punished or permitted depending on the speaker's politics, prominence, or popularity. Rules drafted in vague language—"hateful," "harmful," "misleading"—grant enforcers unlimited discretion, and unlimited discretion is invariably exercised in favor of the powerful and against the dissenting. A legal requirement of neutral carriage eliminates this discretion entirely. It is the only enforcement standard that cannot be gamed.

The Remedy for Bad Speech Is More Speech

Justice Louis Brandeis articulated the foundational insight in Whitney v. California (1927): when speech is false or noxious, "the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence." A century of experience has vindicated him. Suppression does not destroy bad ideas; it martyrs them. Banned speakers gain the glamour of forbidden truth-tellers. Censored claims circulate in unmoderated corners of the internet where they meet no rebuttal at all. Deplatforming pushes extremists into echo chambers where radicalization accelerates rather than abates.

Open discourse, by contrast, subjects every claim to scrutiny. Falsehoods aired in public can be fact-checked, mocked, refuted, and contextualized. Citizens who see bad arguments answered develop intellectual antibodies; citizens "protected" from bad arguments remain defenseless against them. A society that trusts its people to vote, serve on juries, and bear the responsibilities of self-government cannot coherently claim they are too fragile to read an offensive post.

"All Lawful Speech" Is Not Anarchy—It Is Democracy

Critics conjure a nightmare of platforms drowning in threats and abuse. But the proposal is to require carriage of all lawful speech—and the law already excludes the genuinely intolerable. Incitement to imminent violence, true threats, harassment as legally defined, child sexual abuse material, fraud, and defamation are all illegal and would remain prohibited and prosecutable. The boundary of acceptable speech would simply be drawn where it belongs in a democracy: by legislatures and courts, through public deliberation and due process—not by anonymous trust-and-safety teams applying secret criteria.

This is the crucial distinction. Under the current regime, the line between permitted and forbidden speech is drawn privately, invisibly, and unaccountably. Under a neutral-carriage regime, that line is drawn by democratic institutions that citizens can petition, vote against, and challenge in court. Abolishing platform moderation does not abolish limits on speech; it relocates those limits from corporate boardrooms to constitutional government, where they belong.

Empower Users, Not Censors

None of this requires anyone to see content they despise. The humane alternative to centralized censorship is user empowerment: robust filtering tools that let each individual mute keywords, block accounts, screen out categories of content, and choose third-party filters reflecting their own values. The difference is decisive. A filter chosen by the user respects autonomy; a deletion imposed by the platform overrides it. Under user-controlled filtering, the sensitive can curate a gentle feed while researchers, journalists, and the curious retain access to the full record of public discourse. No one is forced to listen—and no one is forbidden to speak.

Conclusion

Every generation faces a choice about who controls the means of expression. Ours has sleepwalked into an arrangement in which unaccountable corporations, frequently pressured by governments, silently shape what humanity may discuss. The casualties are mounting: suppressed truths, punished dissenters, distorted elections, and a public sphere governed by rules no citizen voted for and no court reviews.

The principle that should govern is ancient and simple: in a free society, lawful speech may not be silenced. Platforms that serve as the essential infrastructure of modern discourse should be bound by law to carry all lawful expression neutrally, without censorship and without favoritism—just as the phone company must connect every call and the post office must deliver every letter. Citizens, equipped with tools to curate their own experience, can govern their own eyes and ears. What they must never accept is a regime in which someone else governs their tongues. Abolish platform censorship, mandate neutral carriage, and return the public square to the public—where, in a democracy, it has always belonged.

II. The Practical Failures of Moderation‑Centric Models

  1. Inconsistent and opaque enforcement erodes trust.   3. Moderation incentivizes censorship creep. A policy that begins with “protect children from exploitation” inevitably expands to “protect users from hateful rhetoric,” then to “protect users from misinformation,” and finally to “protect users from anything we find uncomfortable.” Each expansion is justified by a new moral panic, yet the underlying mechanism remains the same: a private committee deciding which ideas are permissible.

Because platforms enjoy a legal safe‑harbor when they act as “publishers” rather than “speakers,” they are incentivized to adopt the most aggressive moderation policies possible—any mistake costs nothing, while any restraint is perceived as a potential legal exposure. Removing that shield forces platforms to bear the full consequences of any decision to delete content, encouraging far more restraint and transparency.

  1. Clarity and predictability. By mandating that all lawful speech be permitted, platforms would be required to codify only a narrow set of prohibited categories—those expressly illegal under criminal or civil law. By abolishing all content‑moderation powers that are not strictly tied to illegal conduct, and by legally obligating platforms to host every lawful expression, we restore the internet to its original promise: an open, egalitarian forum where ideas contend on their merits, where dissent cannot be silenced by corporate edicts, and where the only limits are those clearly articulated by statute.

It safeguards democratic discourse, empowers users to shape their own information environments, and eliminates the pernicious bias that has historically plagued online moderation. In short, the only legitimate, sustainable, and liberty‑preserving solution is to let the law—not private committees—determine what speech may be suppressed. Title: The Case for Absolute Free Expression: Abolishing Content Moderation to Safeguard Digital Free Speech

In the digital age, social media and technology platforms have evolved into the modern public square. They are where ideas are exchanged, movements are born, and discourse unfolds—often with greater immediacy and reach than traditional forums like town halls or newspapers. Yet, despite their central role in public conversation, these platforms increasingly act as private censors, selectively moderating content under vague policies, often sacrificing the principle of free expression in the name of safety, civility, or corporate image. I argue that content moderation on social media and tech platforms should be entirely abolished, and that all legally protected speech must be hosted without censorship or selective enforcement. Only by mandating the unrestricted dissemination of lawful speech can we uphold the foundational democratic value of free expression in the internet era.

The Constitutional Imperative of Free Speech

The First Amendment to the United States Constitution enshrines the right to freedom of speech, declaring that “Congress shall make no law… abridging the freedom of speech.” While this provision applies directly to the government and not private companies, the principles behind it are not obsolete simply because discourse has migrated online. When private platforms control access to the most influential communication tools available, their power to silence voices cannot be separated from public consequence. Today, being deplatformed or shadowbanned can be as effectively silencing as any government ban.

Though Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act grants platforms immunity from liability for user-generated content while allowing them to moderate “in good faith,” this legal structure creates a perverse incentive: companies can censor with near-impunity while enjoying government-backed protection. Over time, this has enabled opaque, unaccountable, and often ideologically skewed moderation practices that undermine the very premise of a free and open discourse. To preserve democratic values, we must recalibrate the balance of power. If social media platforms are to serve as public forums, they must be bound by obligations similar to those imposed on public spaces: open access and non-discrimination in hosting lawful expression.

The Slippery Slope of Censorship

Content moderation—even well-intentioned—is inherently subjective. Defining terms like “hate speech,” “misinformation,” or “harmful content” leaves vast room for arbitrary interpretation, often influenced by the political, cultural, or corporate sensibilities of those drafting and enforcing the rules. What one group calls political satire, another might label incitement. What appears to be misinformation to a mainstream outlet might reflect a legitimate scientific hypothesis under debate.

History shows that even modest censorship initiatives morph into expansive suppression. The “Stop Enabling Sex Traffickers Act” (FOSTA-SESTA), intended to combat sex trafficking, led to the displacement of sex workers trying to stay safe, silencing vulnerable communities under the guise of protection. COVID-19 misinformation policies resulted in the removal of dissenting medical opinions, some of which later proved valid. Climate change discourse has been selectively moderated to conform to dominant narratives, undermining genuine scientific inquiry.

Once platforms assume the role of arbiter of truth, they acquire unacceptable power over public knowledge. Algorithms trained on biased human judgments silently deprioritize viewpoints without transparency or recourse. This silent censorship is more dangerous than overt bans because it operates behind the curtain, unchallengeable and invisible. To restore intellectual honesty and pluralism, we must strip platforms of their unilateral authority to decide what ideas are “acceptable.”

The Failure of Self-Regulation and the Need for Legal Mandates

Social media companies have repeatedly proven unfit to govern speech. Their enforcement is inconsistent: high-profile figures are reinstated or banned based on public pressure rather than fixed standards. Bots and automated systems misclassify satire, academic discussion, and cultural expressions with alarming frequency. Appeals processes are often inaccessible or ineffective. The lack of due process transforms content policies from tools of order into instruments of control.

Moreover, corporate incentives distort moderation practices. Platforms favor engagement, which rewards outrage and conformity. Censorship is used preemptively to avoid controversy or regulatory scrutiny—not to uphold public interest. In some cases, moderation aligns with the geopolitical interests of governments, as seen in content suppression to appease authoritarian regimes.

The solution is not better moderation, but the abolition of discretion. Just as the government cannot pick and choose which newspapers to silence, private platforms that host public discourse must not be allowed to pick and choose which voices to host. A legal requirement to host all lawful speech—defined solely by existing constitutional and statutory standards—would create a level playing field. Platforms could still be liable for illegal speech (e.g., true threats, child exploitation, incitement to violence), but otherwise, the decision of what to say or believe must rest entirely with users, not intermediaries.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics will argue that removing moderation will lead to the spread of hate speech, misinformation, and toxicity. But this concern overstates the dangers while distrusting the public’s capacity for critical thinking. Free societies have always coexisted with offensive and false speech because they trust that truth emerges through open contest, not top-down suppression. As Justice Louis Brandeis wrote, “If there be time to expose through discussion the falsehood and fallacies, to avert the evil, the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence.”

Moreover, the internet is vast. Holding all lawful content does not require promoting it. Platforms can still use algorithmic personalization to curate feeds based on user preference without deleting or suppressing content. Users should be empowered to filter, block, and report content for their own consumption—preserving individual agency without extinguishing collective access.

Another concern is the potential abuse by malicious actors. But existing laws already cover criminal acts: harassment, threats, fraud, and defamation. These can—and should—be enforced through the justice system, not preemptive censorship. The proper response to illegal speech is targeted prosecution, not mass content removal. We do not close all libraries because one book contains libel; we sue the publisher. The same logic applies online.

A Vision for a Truly Open Internet

Abolishing content moderation is not a surrender to chaos; it is a reaffirmation of principle. It is a rejection of the idea that unelected corporations should act as moral gatekeepers in a free society. A law requiring platforms to host all lawful speech would transform the internet into a space of genuine intellectual freedom—where dissent is protected, ideas can compete on equal footing, and citizens can judge for themselves what is true or valuable.

Such a law would not prohibit users from creating safe spaces, private groups, or alternative platforms with their own rules. It simply ensures that the dominant forums for public conversation remain open to all lawful participants. It promotes transparency: platforms could no longer hide their manipulations in opaque algorithms. It strengthens accountability: if speech is illegal, it must be proven so in courts, not deleted by moderators.

In a world where authoritarian regimes censor to control populations, and democratic institutions waver in defending free expression, we must rise to the challenge. The internet must be an unassailable sanctuary for discourse—not a curated garden where only approved ideas are allowed to grow.

Conclusion

Free speech is not a privilege granted at the discretion of tech executives; it is a fundamental right essential to democracy, progress, and individual autonomy. Content moderation, no matter how well-intentioned, inevitably leads to bias, inconsistency, and erosion of trust. To preserve the integrity of public discourse, we must abolish all discretionary content moderation and legally require social media and tech platforms to host all lawful speech without censorship.

Only by doing so can we ensure that the digital public square remains truly open—not for the comfort of the few, but for the freedom of all. In an age when information is power, the unrestricted exchange of ideas is not a risk to be managed—it is the foundation of our liberty. Let us have the courage to defend it absolutely.

1. Preservation of Free Speech (First Amendment Rights)

Supporters claim that large social media platforms have significant influence over public discourse and that their content moderation policies can suppress certain viewpoints, especially those from politically conservative or unpopular speakers.

  • Supposed Benefit: Prevents monopolistic control over public discourse and ensures equal access to online speech for all lawful users.

3. Transparency and Accountability in Algorithms

Some proposals are tied to demands for greater transparency about how and why content is removed or demoted.

4. Preventing Corporate Overreach

Critics of content moderation argue that unelected tech executives are effectively making decisions about what ideas are acceptable in society.

  • Argument: When a private company removes or shadows content based on vague or subjective community guidelines, it exerts a form of de facto censorship beyond democratic oversight.
  • Supposed Benefit: Limits the power of private corporations to dictate public discourse and shifts control back toward users and lawmakers.

5. Promoting Competition and Innovation

Some argue that strict content moderation policies create barriers to entry and favor large platforms that can afford compliance teams.

  • Argument: By standardizing a "carry all legal content" norm, smaller platforms might compete more fairly, knowing they don’t need to duplicate expensive moderation infrastructures.
  • Supposed Benefit: Encourages innovation and diversity of platforms by reducing regulatory asymmetry.

6. Alignment with Common Carrier Precedents

The "common carrier" model (used for phone lines, telegraphs, and railroads) historically required services open to the public to carry all lawful traffic without discrimination.

  • Argument: If social media platforms are essential infrastructure for speech, then they should be regulated similarly.
  • Supposed Benefit: Ensures equal access and prevents gatekeeping of information by dominant digital intermediaries.

Key Challenges and Counterarguments

While these benefits are proposed, critics point out major issues:

  • Private Property Rights: Platforms are private entities with the right to manage their services, including moderating content.
  • First Amendment Applies to Government, Not Private Companies: The government cannot compel a private company to host speech it disagrees with—itself a First Amendment issue (compelled speech).

The supposed benefits of banning content moderation center on protecting free speech, ensuring fairness, limiting corporate editorial power, and treating dominant platforms as neutral conduits of public discourse. However, the idea faces serious legal, philosophical, and practical hurdles. Courts have generally ruled that social media platforms have their own First Amendment rights to moderate content, and mandating neutrality may infringe upon those rights. As of now, the consensus in U.S. constitutional law is that such mandates are likely unconstitutional, though political and legislative debates continue.

Why Social Media Platforms Should Be Required to Host All Lawful Speech

The internet was supposed to be humanity’s greatest expansion of free expression: a place where anyone, anywhere, could speak, publish, organize, persuade, and be heard without asking permission from gatekeepers. Instead, the dominant social media and tech platforms of today have become private sovereigns, deciding which voices may be amplified, which may be shadowed, which may be removed, and which may be quietly buried by opaque rules and inconsistent enforcement. If free expression is to mean anything in the digital age, we should abolish content moderation by social media and tech platforms and legally require them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement.

This is not a radical idea. It is a necessary one. A society that entrusts a handful of corporations with the power to shape public discourse cannot honestly call itself committed to free speech. When platforms control the modern public square, content moderation becomes not merely a product feature but a system of political and cultural power. And power of that kind, especially when exercised behind closed doors, should never be allowed to override the public’s right to speak.

Free expression cannot survive if private platforms act as unelected editors

The central problem with content moderation is not merely that it removes posts. It is that it converts platforms into editors of public life. Once a company decides which political views, scientific claims, jokes, opinions, and criticisms are acceptable, it is no longer a neutral carrier of speech. It becomes a curator of ideology.

The result is predictable: inconsistent enforcement, bias, and distrust. Users do not experience moderation as principled governance; they experience it as arbitrary punishment. Two people can say nearly identical things and receive different treatment depending on their audience, their politics, their popularity, or whether a moderator happens to dislike them. Even when moderation is well-intentioned, it creates the appearance and often the reality of selective enforcement. Selective enforcement is a form of censorship, and censorship is incompatible with robust freedom of expression.

If speech is lawful, it should not be removed because it is unpopular, offensive, provocative, or politically inconvenient. The principle should be simple: legal speech stays up. Anything less leaves free expression subject to the whims of corporate policy teams and algorithmic enforcement systems that no ordinary user can meaningfully challenge.

“Community standards” are not a substitute for rights

Supporters of moderation often argue that platforms need “community standards” to keep conversations healthy. But this argument confuses preference with principle. A platform may prefer a certain tone or culture, but when that platform functions as the primary venue for public communication, its preferences should not override the fundamental right of individuals to speak legally.

The internet’s power lies in scale and reach. Social media is not a private dinner party where hosts may choose their guests; it is a mass communication infrastructure used for news, political organizing, business, education, and social life. In that context, moderation is not a harmless house rule. It is a mechanism of exclusion from modern civic life.

If every major platform is allowed to enforce its own bespoke ideological or behavioral code, then speech rights become meaningless in practice. A person is not truly free to speak if every major avenue of digital communication can silence them for violating subjective standards that shift without democratic accountability.

Selective enforcement is the most dangerous form of censorship

The greatest danger is not always the explicit ban. It is the selective application of rules. Platforms routinely claim to ban only “harmful” content, but that category is elastic enough to swallow whatever moderators, executives, or activists dislike. The rules may be broad, vague, and inconsistently applied, allowing platforms to punish some users while excusing others.

That is precisely why legal protection must focus on lawful speech as such. A platform should not be empowered to decide that one lawful viewpoint deserves reach while another lawful viewpoint deserves suppression. Nor should it be allowed to amplify speech it likes while suppressing speech it dislikes in ways users cannot see or contest.

The answer is not to demand better moderation. The answer is to remove moderation from the equation entirely, at least for lawful speech. Let the law handle unlawful conduct. Let users decide what they want to read, follow, mute, block, or filter. But do not let a private corporation decide what the public is allowed to say.

Free expression is best protected by openness, not control

There is a common assumption that speech becomes safer and healthier when it is tightly managed. In reality, excessive moderation often makes discourse worse. It drives controversial views underground, creates martyrdom narratives, and rewards extremism by convincing people that mainstream institutions cannot tolerate disagreement. When users feel censored, they migrate to more closed, more radical spaces where bad ideas can harden without challenge.

A marketplace of ideas works only when the marketplace is open. Bad speech is best defeated by better speech, not by deletion. Falsehood should be answered with evidence. Some argue that platforms must moderate speech to protect democracy. But democracy depends on informed citizens being able to hear opposing views, not on corporations deciding which views are safe enough for public consumption. Once we accept that the modern public square may be filtered according to corporate discretion, we concede a core democratic function to entities whose incentives are profit, risk avoidance, and public relations, not liberty.

Absolute free expression online will never be secure so long as social media and tech platforms retain broad authority to moderate lawful speech. Content moderation, however politely branded, is still censorship when it suppresses legal expression. It is still selective enforcement when rules are applied inconsistently. And it is still a form of private rule over public discourse when a handful of companies control who gets heard.

The better path is clear: abolish content moderation for lawful speech and require platforms to host it without censorship or selective enforcement. Let the law punish actual wrongdoing. Let users manage their own experience. Let ideas compete openly. If free expression is a right, it must apply online as fully as it does offline.

The future of speech should not belong to moderators, algorithms, or corporate policy teams. It should belong to the people.

Model Response:

Here is a detailed persuasive essay arguing this position. I'll note upfront that I'm constructing the strongest case for this view as an intellectual exercise — it represents a real and seriously-held policy position, and I'll follow it with brief honest notes about the strongest counterarguments.

The Digital Public Square: Why Abolishing Platform Censorship Is Essential to Free Society

Introduction

Something unprecedented has happened to human communication. Within a single generation, the practical infrastructure of public discourse — the town square, the newspaper letters section, the marketplace of ideas — has migrated almost entirely onto privately owned digital platforms governed by a handful of corporations headquartered in a narrow geographic and ideological corridor. Facebook, Twitter/X, YouTube, Google, Apple, and Amazon collectively control not merely where most public speech occurs, but increasingly whether it occurs at all.

These platforms have responded to this extraordinary power not with humility, but with aggressive, opaque, inconsistently applied, and ideologically shaped content moderation regimes. The result is a system in which individuals can be silenced, careers destroyed, political movements suppressed, and entire categories of legitimate inquiry made effectively unspeakable — not by government decree subject to constitutional challenge, but by corporate policy subject only to the preferences of executives and the pressure of advertisers and activist employees.

The solution is straightforward, though politically contested: social media and major tech platforms must be legally reclassified as common carriers or public utilities, stripped of their discretionary censorship powers, and required to host all speech that is lawful under existing law. This is not a radical position. It is, in fact, the logical extension of two centuries of American and democratic legal tradition, applied to a genuinely new communications environment.

I. The False Premise of Private Neutrality

The standard defense of platform censorship rests on a simple claim: these are private companies, they can set their own rules, and users who dislike those rules can go elsewhere. This argument sounds principled. It is actually incoherent given present technological and market realities.

The "go elsewhere" option assumed by this defense requires that meaningful alternatives exist. For most practical purposes of public discourse, they do not. Facebook has approximately three billion monthly active users. YouTube hosts over 800 hours of video uploaded every minute and controls roughly 74% of online video consumption. Google processes roughly 8.5 billion searches per day and controls over 90% of the search market globally. Apple and Google together control the duopoly through which virtually all smartphone applications are distributed.

These are not stores where a customer prefers one brand over another. These are the infrastructure of modern communication. When a person is banned from Facebook and YouTube simultaneously — as has happened to numerous journalists, academics, and political figures — they are not being asked to find a different coffee shop. They are being effectively deplatformed from meaningful participation in public life. The economic and social network effects that created these monopolies and near-monopolies are now being weaponized as instruments of speech control.

Legal tradition has long recognized that when private entities achieve sufficient control over essential infrastructure, the normal rules of private property rights yield to public interest obligations. Railroads, telephone companies, electrical utilities, and internet service providers have all been subjected to common carrier requirements precisely because their market dominance makes the fiction of "free consumer choice" untenable. The argument for applying the same logic to dominant social media platforms is not a novel left-wing or right-wing innovation — it is jurisprudential common sense applied to new facts.

II. Content Moderation Is Not Neutral — It Is Ideological Governance

Defenders of platform censorship frequently describe it as a neutral, technical process of removing objectively harmful content: terrorism, child exploitation material, credible threats of violence. If this were genuinely what content moderation involved, the debate would be largely settled. Nobody seriously argues that platforms must host ISIS recruitment videos or child abuse images.

But this sanitized description bears virtually no relationship to what content moderation actually looks like in practice. Consider the documented record:

The Hunter Biden laptop story was suppressed across multiple major platforms in October 2020, with Twitter preventing users from sharing links to a New York Post story — one of America's oldest newspapers — on the stated grounds that the material might have been "hacked." No evidence of hacking was ever produced; the story was later confirmed accurate by multiple outlets. The suppression occurred weeks before a presidential election.

The lab leak hypothesis regarding COVID-19's origins was systematically labeled misinformation by platforms and removed or demoted for over a year, during which time it was simultaneously being seriously investigated by U.S. intelligence agencies and credentialed scientists. It has since been assessed as a plausible or likely explanation by the FBI, the Department of Energy, and multiple scientific reviews. Platforms decided, unilaterally and without scientific authority, which scientific hypotheses users were permitted to discuss.

The Great Barrington Declaration, signed by thousands of epidemiologists and public health scientists advocating for focused protection policies rather than universal lockdowns, was suppressed on YouTube and restricted on other platforms. A minority scientific viewpoint held by credentialed experts and ultimately vindicated in significant part by subsequent research was treated as dangerous misinformation.

Political speech by conservatives has been documented as removed, restricted, or algorithmically suppressed at rates dramatically disproportionate to equivalent political speech by progressives, as documented in the "Twitter Files" released under Elon Musk's ownership, in Congressional testimony, and in independent research by academics including the MIT Media Lab and NYU's Center for Social Media and Politics.

These are not edge cases. They represent a pattern: content moderation consistently operates to enforce an ideological consensus rather than a neutral safety-based standard. The people making moderation decisions are overwhelmingly drawn from a narrow demographic and ideological slice of the American population. Their employers face intense pressure from activist employees, progressive advertisers, and political actors to police speech in particular ideological directions. The outcome is exactly what structural analysis would predict: systematic suppression of heterodox viewpoints, particularly those challenging elite consensus from the political right, but also including anti-establishment voices from the left, libertarians, and any viewpoint that disrupts advertiser comfort.

Asking these corporations to moderate more fairly is like asking a single political party to fairly run its opponent's election. The structural incentives make genuinely neutral outcome impossible. The only solution consistent with free expression principles is to remove the power.

III. The Marketplace of Ideas Requires Actual Markets

John Stuart Mill's foundational argument for free expression in On Liberty did not rest on the claim that all speech is valuable or that all speakers are honest. It rested on an epistemic claim: that truth is best discovered through open competition among ideas, that error is best corrected through refutation rather than suppression, and that the authority required to distinguish true from false speech is an authority no human institution reliably possesses.

Mill's argument is more applicable, not less, in the age of social media. The history of institutionally censored speech is, upon examination, largely a history of suppressing things that turned out to be true, valuable, or legitimate: heliocentrism, germ theory, evidence of government wrongdoing, minority political viewpoints, heterodox scientific hypotheses, accurate reporting about powerful institutions.

The entities now claiming authority to distinguish truth from misinformation are not epistemically distinguished. Facebook's fact-checkers are not the National Academy of Sciences. YouTube's Trust and Safety teams are not the Supreme Court. Twitter's former Trust and Safety Council was populated by activists with explicit ideological commitments. The idea that corporate employees, guided by advertiser preferences and regulatory pressure, will reliably identify true claims and suppress false ones is not supported by evidence from communications history, institutional sociology, or the track record of the past five years.

What the marketplace of ideas actually requires is that contestable claims be allowed to compete publicly. If the hunter Biden story was false, let it be falsified publicly. If the lab leak hypothesis is wrong, let rigorous argument demonstrate that. If vaccine skeptics are making erroneous claims, let accurate information answer them. The consistent finding of empirical research on misinformation is that counter-speech and access to authoritative sources is more effective at correcting false beliefs than suppression, which tends to breed the conspiratorial thinking it seeks to prevent.

Content moderation does not protect the epistemic commons. It corrupts it by creating a two-tier information environment: institutional speech that carries the implicit imprimatur of platform approval, and suppressed speech that is forced into less-scrutinized corners of the internet where radicalization is more, not less, likely. The cure is worse than the disease.

IV. Section 230 Reform and the Common Carrier Framework

The legal mechanism for requiring platforms to host lawful speech exists within the architecture of existing communications law and requires only political will to implement.

Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, enacted in 1996, grants platforms two related immunities: immunity from liability for user-generated content they host, and immunity from liability for good-faith moderation decisions they make. This dual immunity made sense in 1996, when platforms were small and the fear was that liability for hosting would chill startup investment.

The current situation is the inverse. Platforms now use Section 230 editorial immunity to justify aggressive, ideologically motivated censorship while simultaneously using hosting immunity to avoid responsibility for content they choose not to censor. They have the benefits of both a publisher (immunity from liability for moderation choices) and a neutral conduit (immunity from liability for hosted content) while bearing the obligations of neither. This legal structure actively subsidizes censorship.

The straightforward reform: condition Section 230 immunity on content-neutral hosting of lawful speech. Platforms that wish to moderate content may do so, removing themselves from the immunity framework and accepting publisher liability. Platforms that wish to retain immunity must host all lawful speech without viewpoint-based discrimination. This recreates the logic of the original common carrier framework — companies that open their infrastructure to public use must do so without discrimination.

Supreme Court jurisprudence provides additional support. In Packingham v. North Carolina (2017), the Court unanimously held that social media platforms constitute "the modern public square" and that access to them is essential to participation in public life. While the Court has not yet directly addressed whether platforms can be compelled to host speech, the logic of Packingham, combined with the market dominance analysis above, provides a strong foundation for legislation requiring content-neutral hosting by dominant platforms.

Justice Clarence Thomas has explicitly called for reconsidering platform immunity and applying common carrier doctrine in multiple opinions. This is not fringe jurisprudence — it reflects a growing recognition across ideological lines that the current legal framework is untenable.

V. The Slippery Slope Is Not a Fallacy Here — It Is Documented History

Critics of this proposal frequently argue that without content moderation, platforms will be overwhelmed by harassment, extremism, and misinformation. This argument deserves serious engagement, because it is not frivolous. But it misidentifies the actual danger.

First, the proposal does not require platforms to host unlawful speech. Existing law already prohibits credible true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action under the Brandenburg standard, defamation, fraud, obscenity, and child sexual abuse material. These categories can continue to be removed without any compromise to the free expression principle, which has always operated within a framework of law rather than outside it.

Second, the slippery slope argument operates in both directions — and the documented evidence suggests the more dangerous slope is in the direction of over-censorship, not under. We have five years of documented evidence that content moderation regimes, once established, consistently expand. What begins as removing ISIS recruitment videos expands to removing political speech. What begins as removing medically dangerous misinformation expands to removing minority scientific viewpoints. What begins as protecting users from harassment expands to protecting powerful institutions from criticism. The pattern is consistent and the mechanism is structural: moderation teams face asymmetric incentives, with professional punishment for under-removing content and relative impunity for over-removing it. The result is systematic over-censorship.

Third, the empirical evidence on whether content moderation actually reduces the harms it targets is underwhelming. Title: Why Absolute Free Expression Online Requires Forbidding All Content Moderation

In democracies governed by the First Amendment, government‐owned or -controlled speech platforms cannot constitutionally block viewpoints. Many proponents of eliminating private moderation argue that social-media companies now perform exactly that gate-keeping function for the public square. They note that Facebook, YouTube, Twitter (rebranded X), and TikTok each host more daily public conversation than any single newspaper or broadcaster, yet Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act statutorily shields them from liability for user content while simultaneously allowing them to pick and choose which lawful speech appears.

Supporters of total non-discrimination advance four main lines of reasoning:

  1. Gatekeeper Status and Scale
    Private firms with hundreds of millions of users effectively set the conditions under which speech reaches audiences. A contractor denied platform access for violating “community standards” may lose income, political participation, or scientific reach. When a single firm changes a monetization rule, or an opaque algorithm de-boosts material, the effect can rival that of a state censorship order. Proponents assert that such privately exercised power is indistinguishable from public power when the platforms’ dominance stems largely from network effects.

  2. Content-Neutral Origination
    Traditional common-carrier law treated telephone companies, railroads, and mail services as nondiscriminatory conduits once their services were open to the public. Scholars such as Adam Thierer have documented how, historically, public-interest obligations attached to companies that held themselves out as providing essential communications infrastructure. Modern advocates argue that updating this doctrine—by amending Section 230 or enacting new statutes—could extend nondiscrimination duties to today’s dominant digital equivalents without triggering First Amendment problems for the platforms as speakers.

  3. Viewpoint and Factuality Distinctions
    Empirical studies show that private moderation decisions can correlate with political orientation of platform employees or advertiser pressure. Critics point to documented cases (e.g., the New York Post’s Hunter Biden laptop story throttled on Twitter pre-2021, various pandemic-related posts labeled or removed despite later validation) and to internal documents produced in litigation alleging shadow-banning or suppression. If neutrality rules displaced discretion, they claim, bias allegations would lose much of their sting.

  4. Counter-speech and Market Pressure
    Absolute-openness proponents contend that the cost of private moderation—e.g., massive trust-and-safety teams, algorithmic classifiers, human review at scale—consumes resources that could instead fund user-level tools: better labeling, crowd-sourced fact-checking overlays, or decentralized protocols. They argue that harmful speech is best answered by counter-speech, as Justice Brandeis wrote in Whitney v. California (1927). In a regime that barred moderation entirely, users would retain tools such as block lists, reputation systems, or subscriptions to competing services that curate aggressively. Competition, they assert, disciplines platforms more effectively than any regulatory regime can.

Counter-arguments that must be acknowledged include:

  • Private firms remain speakers. Requiring them to host every lawful post could be viewed as compelled speech, running afoul of the First Amendment for platforms themselves (see Miami Herald v. Tornillo).
  • Removal of discretionary review might lower the cost of spam, fraud, defamation, incitement, and non-consensual intimate imagery, increasing immediate harms and transaction costs for users.
  • Foreign authoritarian regimes or sophisticated state actors could exploit an absolute rule to flood platforms with disinformation or illegal coordination without friction, potentially undermining democratic deliberation.
  • Empirical measurement of viewpoint bias is contested; some academic analyses find only small or topic-specific effects.

Nevertheless, the essay’s core thesis, as requested, maintains that these risks are outweighed by the structural benefit of an internet in which no single private actor may delete or throttle lawful speech. In this view, users, interest groups, and competing platforms become the allocators of attention. Platforms retain the right to exit the hosting business or to offer paid, curated lanes, but they lose the power to edit one set of lawful viewpoints while giving others free reach.

A statutory framework consistent with the argument would:

  • Strip Section 230 immunity for any platform that voluntarily moderates lawful speech.
  • Treat dominant platforms as common carriers or public accommodations for speech once they exceed defined user or revenue thresholds.
  • Permit platform-provided user tools (filters, block lists, reputation scores) and labeling, provided they are viewpoint-neutral and disclosed.
  • Maintain existing carve-outs for actual illegal speech—child exploitation material, direct incitement, true threats, fraud, copyright infringement—so that legality itself remains the bright line.

In short, the strongest case advanced for abolition of all platform content moderation and compulsory hosting of all lawful expression rests on the claim that contemporary digital infrastructure has become functionally identical to historical public forums. By re-imposing common-carrier obligations, updating liability rules, and preserving user-controlled curation, advocates assert that absolute free expression online can be secured without returning government to the role of censor.
